text: The authors report that repairing (rather than salvaging) corrupted compressed data had received little research; existing tools mostly extract the uncorrupted parts.
quote: Repairing compressed data has not been subject to significant research efforts, with tools mostly focused on extracting uncorrupted fragments from corrupted archives.

text: Repair treats the zlib Adler-32 check as a black-box oracle: each single-bit-flip mutation of a corrupted compressed fragment is tested for validity.
quote: by modeling the Adler32 check as an oracle, querying it with a repair candidate, a compressed fragment to which a bitflip is applied

text: Bit-flip search repair raised the recovered share of a real, corrupted SquashFS image from 8.32% (stock squashfs-tools) to 99.68% of bits.
quote: Overall, the repair process manages to increase the ratio of recovered data from 8.32% to 99.68%

text: Under the single-bit-flip model, 3 corrupted fragments kept more than one candidate after the inflate, Adler-32 and length filters, so a passing checksum did not identify a unique repair.
quote: repaired with a single bitflip (cardinality of target candidates is zero), while 3 have multiple targets

text: Under the double-bit-flip model, the number of surviving candidate repairs per fragment ranged from 1 to 40717.
quote: The number of target candidates for each fragment ranges from 1 up to 40717

text: Ambiguous repairs are merged with three-valued logic: a bit is kept only where all surviving candidates agree, otherwise it is marked indeterminate instead of being guessed.
quote: a bit is of value true (respectively false) if and only if this bit is equal to true (respectively false) in all target candidates, otherwise it is of value indeterminate

text: Choosing between a few candidate repairs was done by an expert with binary diffing, manually and separately for each fragment.
quote: This process is entirely manual, time consuming, and needs to be performed from scratch for

text: Exhaustive double-bit-flip search cost from 22 days to more than a year of CPU time per fragment.
quote: All fragments have been repaired: the smallest takes 22 days, while the biggest takes more than a year.

text: Repair of stream compression (LZMA), where one flip corrupts everything after it, is left as future work; only block-wise compression is handled.
quote: The rest of this paper only focuses on block compression, by detailing the process to repair the corrupted SquashFS filesystem, leaving stream compression for future work.

text: Damage in the real NAND dump is modelled as independent, identically distributed bit flips (a Bernoulli model) whose rate is estimated from the dump itself.
quote: In the rest of this paper, a Bernoulli error model of parameter p is used to more precisely quantify the bitflips.

text: In a real Google Home flash dump read without usable ECC, 204 of 920 gzip-compressed fragments (22%) failed to decompress.
quote: The squashfs-tools utility fails at decompressing 204 out of the 920 fragments (22%) of the filesystem.

text: File repair is framed as two objectives: keep as much of the original's information as possible (omission) and introduce as little new information as possible (fabrication).
quote: a successful file repair must optimize two parameters: It must contain as much information of the original file as possible and introduce as little information that is not contained in the original as possible

text: Force Open changes the viewer's execution (forcing branches learned from valid files) rather than the damaged file itself.
quote: Force Open does not modify the file but instead modifies the execution of the file viewer, forcing it to open a corrupted file.

text: On PDFs (viewer: pdftotext), every file Force Open managed to open produced text identical to the original's extraction; its PDF repairs were all-or-nothing.
quote: For all files that were successfully opened, the Levenshtein distance of the produced output to the output of pdftotext with the original file as input is zero

text: The sets of PDFs repaired by Force Open and by pdftk overlap little, so the two tools are complementary.
quote: the overlap of repaired documents is again small (Fig. 4c & Table 1), i.e. our approach repairs additional files and could thus be used as additional heuristic to improve the overall results.

text: Adding Force Open to the reference tool raised the number of repaired files by 31.30% for PDF (84.82% for PNG, 35.92% for JPG).
quote: The total number of repaired files on average increases by 84.82% for PNG files, 35.92% for JPG files, and 31.30% for PDF files.

text: Evaluation damage is synthetic: n random bytes overwrite a random position, and the copy is kept only if the viewer then fails to open it.
quote: overwrites the n bytes starting at that position with random data. It then tries to open the modified copy with the specified program.

text: Force Open cannot repair data-dependent corruption (for example image dimensions) that is not expressed as a simple branch.
quote: Force Open is not capable of repairing corruptions that are highly data dependant (e.g. image dimensions) and are not in the form of some if-then-else statement.

text: Because it bypasses integrity checks, the approach opens a path for malicious exploitation and must be sandboxed.
quote: Our approach is designed to circumvent integrity checks and as such also introduces a possibility for malicious exploitation.

text: After partial overwriting, it may be impossible to tell which recovered data are original and which are overwriting data.
quote: Deleted data might be completely overwritten or only partially overwritten. It may not be possible to determine what data are original and what have been overwritten.

text: NIST CFTT testing found that file-carving and deleted-file-recovery results can miss data or mix data from multiple sources.
quote: Deleted file recovery and file carving results need to be carefully examined and might contain missing data or data mixed from multiple sources.

text: NIST's taxonomy of tool inaccuracy includes 'existence' errors: a faulty tool may report data that were not present in the original.
quote: Existence: Do all artifacts reported as present exist? For example, a faulty tool might add data that were not present in the original.

text: The taxonomy also includes 'association' errors: a tool links information from one item to a different, unrelated item.
quote: A faulty tool might incorrectly associate information pertaining to one item with a different, unrelated item.

text: CFTT scores file-carving tools by how much of the original file is returned, how much is omitted and how much returned data is not from the original.
quote: an examination of the data returned to see how much of the original file is returned, how many data are omitted and how many are not from the original file

text: CFTT's static test data sets cover carving of graphic and video files, metadata-based deleted-file recovery and string search; no document format is listed.
quote: The tool functions that use a static data set are file carving for graphic and video files, metadata-based deleted file recovery, and string searching.

text: There are no generally agreed requirements, and no formal standard, to test forensic tools against.
quote: There are no generally agreed requirements for each forensic task, i.e., no formal standard to test against.

text: Digital tools tend to fail systematically (under particular conditions) rather than randomly, so an error-mitigation analysis, not a single error rate, is the right way to manage uncertainty.
quote: Digital processes tend to have systematic errors rather than random errors. Therefore, an error mitigation analysis provides more information and is the correct way to manage uncertainty.

text: Hash-comparing a recovered file with the original gives only pass/fail and cannot tell a near miss from a total failure; graded quality measures are more useful.
quote: However, this only gives a yes or no answer and does not measure whether the recovered file is a total failure or a near miss.

text: NIST lists better sharing of forensic reference data, vital for tool testing, among areas needing further work.
quote: Better sharing of forensic reference data. High-quality testing data are expensive to produce but are vital for tool testing

quote: Such clusters can be detected by appending their data to the end of the damaged compressed stream and the absence of errors during the subsequent decompressing of the resulting fragment

text: When exactly one cluster of an element is missing, the stored CRC-32 of the uncompressed element identifies the correct candidate.
quote: it is possible to define the skipped fragment by calculating the CRC-32 hashes of the uncompressed data stream of this local element.

text: A DEFLATE continuation test alone admits false positives, because almost any bitstream appended to a valid prefix can decode; a structural (XML) filter is needed.

quote: it was possible to achieve an efficiency rate of 82.97 % for document reconstruction on two datasets in total

text: The evaluation is simplified: the search space is thousands of times smaller than a real disk, and all fragments are known in advance to come from one document.

text: The authors call for new mechanisms to verify decompressed XML elements, since effectiveness depends on that verification.

quote: LLM-based verification may yield false positives or false negatives for single-character CIDs or when contextual information is limited.

quote: the task of recovering the document is equivalent to the simpler task of recovering the Unicode translation table

text: Frequency (n-gram) decipherment of CID strings is named as possible but not pursued because endangered languages lack language models.
quote: Such a content lends itself to statistical analysis, where the frequency of CID and character ngrams could be used to recover the encoding.

text: The author rules out the statistical approach for lack of language models for endangered languages.
quote: However, because of the general unavailability of language models for endangered languages this approach is not possible.

text: Per Stefanovitch, the DAS system (SRC-0400) relies on OCR for a subset of well-supported languages and needs extensive training material.
quote: it relies on OCR of the document for a subset of well supported languages, requiring extensive training material

text: Users had to type 4 to 5% of the words for full recovery.
quote: The number of words required by the system is between 4 to 5 % of the total

text: Devanagari: the i-matra is stored after its consonant in Unicode but drawn before it, and extraction follows glyph position, so order must be repaired.
quote: the long vowel "i" is written in a Unicode text string after the character of the consonant it is attached to, but it is displayed before it when the string is visually rendered

text: Vertical Mongolian: extraction tools assume horizontal lines and cannot recover the lines at all.
quote: because PDF documents consider that lines are going exclusively from left to right or right to left, the text extraction tool is totally unable to recover the lines

text: Of 4 UDHR documents without Unicode text, 2 were fully recovered; the others need script-specific development.
quote: We applied this approach to 4 documents of the UDHR corpus for which there exists no Unicode text, 2 of which where fully recovered

text: Future work: train ad-hoc OCR for any script from Unicode-chart symbols with augmentation, for image-only documents.
quote: in order to train ad-hoc OCR system for any scripts solely based on the symbols present in the Unicode charts

text: Endangered-language documents often use ad-hoc, unpublished fonts, a real-world source of non-Unicode encodings.
quote: In order to write in these languages the creators of the documents must design their own ad-hoc fonts, which are not publicly available.

text: Real corrupted fonts map distinct glyphs to the same character (many-to-one) as well as omitting mappings.
quote: Note how both the glyph of the number 2 and of the Cyrillic letter En with hook are both translated to the same character.

text: Under character perturbation (English), WER degrades by up to 6.9 pp for general VLMs, 0.1–3.4 pp for OCR-specialized VLMs and under 0.8 pp for traditional OCR.
quote: VLMs degrade by up to 6.9 points, OCR-specialized VLMs by 0.1–3.4 points, and traditional OCR by less than 0.8 points on English

text: Rewriting of perturbed words: Gemini-3-Flash 0.00%, Qwen3.5-4B 27.35%, olmOCR-2-7B 58.63% (scramble, English).
quote: Rewrite rates vary widely across VLMs, from 0.00% for Gemini-3-Flash and 1.65% for Gemini2.5-Flash to 27.35% for Qwen3.5-4B and 58.63%

text: Perturbing about 5% of characters raises errors on untouched text by up to 7.3 times (general VLMs).
quote: Perturbing ∼5% of characters also increases errors on the remaining unperturbed text by up to 7.3×

text: A no-correction prompt cuts degradation by roughly 30–50% but does not eliminate it.
quote: The instruction does not eliminate degradation but reduces its magnitude by roughly 30–50% across perturbation types.

text: Other scripts such as Arabic and Devanagari were not tested.
quote: behavior may differ for other scripts (e.g., Arabic, Devanagari) or specialized domains

text: Perturbations are controlled manipulations on synthetically rendered PDFs, not natural degradations.
quote: represent controlled manipulations rather than naturally occurring text degradations such as scanning artifacts

text: For literal transcription (legal, forensics), the authors recommend traditional OCR or carefully selected OCR-specialized VLMs.
quote: For applications that require literal transcription, such as legal document processing, historical manuscript digitization, and forensics, traditional OCR systems or carefully selected OCR-specialized VLMs remain the safest choice

text: Existing OCR/document benchmarks (incl. OmniDocBench) measure clean text and cannot detect rewriting.
quote: focus on clean text recognition and are therefore insufficient for investigating how models can handle imperfect inputs

text: Rewriting rate is length dependent: up to 10% for 4–6 character words and 0% from 8 characters.
quote: short words (4–6 characters) are rewritten up to 10% of the time, with a sharp cutoff at 8 characters above which rewriting drops to 0%

text: A token counts as correctly extracted if its Levenshtein ratio to ground truth is at least 0.7.
quote: we use the number of extracted tokens whose Levenshtein Ratio is larger or equal to 0.7

text: Collated-token accuracy is deliberately lenient.
quote: Separate tokens serve to compute a strict score for token-level extraction quality, whereas collated tokens yield a more lenient score

text: DocBank ground truth was itself produced by PDF text extractors (PDFPlumber, PDFMiner).
quote: the dataset creators used PDFPlumber and PDFMiner to extract and annotate relevant content elements by their color

text: Most PDF text-extraction work does not specify ground truth or metrics (citing Mao et al.).
quote: most approaches for text extraction from PDF do not specify the ground-truth data and performance metrics they use, which impedes performance comparisons

text: Bast and Korzen's benchmark scored spurious and missing words, paragraphs and new lines for 14 tools on about 10K documents.
quote: which evaluated spurious and missing words, paragraphs, and new lines for 14 tools but used a comparably small dataset of approx. 10K documents

text: PDF extraction benchmarks are rarely repeated or updated although tools change often.
quote: Few such works exist and were rarely repeated or updated, which is sub-optimal given that many tools receive updates frequently.

text: Future work: diversify disciplines, document types and content elements beyond arXiv LaTeX.
quote: we see further diversification of the collection in terms of disciplines, document types, and content elements as a valuable task for future research

text: Our reading: with the 0.7 Levenshtein-ratio threshold and ratio = 1 - lev/(|a|+|b|) (their Gary/Yuta example implies substitution cost 2), a 5-letter word with one wrong glyph mapping scores 0.8 and counts as correct; token matching is also order-free. The metric cannot see single-glyph fabrication.

Our reading: CPR's validator rewards 'natural' text, i.e. the same language prior that makes VLMs rewrite (SRC-0422); decoding settings, seeds and model checksum are not reported, so neither fabrication rate nor determinism (charter 3c) can be assessed.
CPR's baselines are four web repair services (PDF24, pdf4me, pdfonline, iLovePDF); no open-source engine is compared.
quote: four widely used and publicly accessible PDF repair tools were selected as baselines
